ops.title: gt sync reaches into sibling worktrees with 'git reset --keep', and reports failure at exit 0
ops.body:
Measured 2026-08-01 against real gt 1.8.6 by intercepting every git call from `gt sync --no-interactive`:

```
GIT: fetch --no-write-fetch-head --progress --no-tags -f origin refs/heads/main:refs/gt-fetch-head/main
GIT: rev-parse refs/gt-fetch-head/main
GIT: update-ref refs/remotes/origin/main b6f3974...
GIT: merge-base --is-ancestor main b6f3974...
GIT: -C /…/gt-main-co reset -q --keep b6f3974... --
```

Three durable facts:

1. gt WRITES `refs/remotes/<remote>/<trunk>` itself from its own fetch, before it attempts to move the local branch — so the remote-tracking ref is the oracle gt itself treats as ground truth. This is why ccx vcs restack compares against it rather than the local ref.

2. gt does NOT hit gits "cannot force update the branch used by worktree" refusal, because it does not use `git branch -f`. It runs `git -C <sibling-worktree> reset -q --keep` — i.e. it hard-resets ANOTHER working copys tree without asking. On a clean sibling this SUCCEEDS and local trunk advances. A common assumption that git protects a checked-out branch from gt is therefore wrong.

3. When that reset fails (dirty sibling), gt prints `ERROR: Cannot pull trunk due to conflicting unstaged changes.` and STILL EXITS 0. Same for `WARNING: main could not be fast-forwarded.` Any wrapper that reads gts exit code alone sees success. This is the same class as gts `Did not restack branch <b> …` skip message, also printed to stdout at exit 0.

Fact 2 is gt behavior ccx does not control and should not paper over; it is recorded so nobody re-derives it. Facts 1 and 3 are why restack.go compares against the remote-tracking ref and surfaces gts own ERROR/WARNING lines.
